newsitem.title: USA: China corn sales seen slicing US exports--analysts.
newsitem.headline: China corn sales seen slicing US exports--analysts.

text.p: China's new status as an exporter of corn and Argentina's expected huge crop could slice U.S. corn exports by as much as four million tonnes during the remainder of the marketing year, grain analysts said.
"We may be near the top of U.S. corn exports for the marketing year as our competition with South America and China grows," said Dan Basse, grain analyst with AgResources.
Analysts said U.S. exporters could lose as much as three to four million tonnes of business to China and Argentina. The bulk of the losses will likely come after April, Basse said.
On Thursday, the U.S. Department of Agriculture reported higher than expected net weekly corn export sales of 1.261 million tonnes, and corn prices responded with a rally.

But analysts said that the figure doesn't reflect China's recent sales and the pace of exports is likely to drop as the marketing year progresses and corn from other exporting countries becomes available. The U.S. corn marketing year ends August 31.
Most in the trade had anticipated corn exports from China this year, but forecasts for how much grain China will ship vary wildly as analysts struggle to come up with answers.
"I think one of the most important things is that we're going to have to monitor their volume," said Don Roose, analyst with U.S. Commodities.
"They (China) do have excess stocks right now, and they almost doubled their carryover from last year," he said.

Analyst's estimates for Chinese corn exports for the 1996/97 crop year range from 500,000 tonnes to four million tonnes, with most pegging exports between one and two million tonnes. USDA earlier this month projected 500,000 tonnes.
Market conditions are right for China to reenter export markets because nearby corn contracts are trading at an inverse, where March holds a premium to May, Roose said.
The ongoing lack of farmer selling of old crop corn in the U.S. also means that China can seize the opportunity to sell grain to countries that typically buy U.S., Roose said.
"They (China) can be the substitute for the lack of farmer selling in the U.S.," Roose said.

Many of the recent export sales to China have been optional origin and that trend was expected to continue. Optional origin corn sales leave the exporter with the opportunity to source the purchase from the U.S., Argentina or China, analysts said.

During the past week, China has been selling No. 3 yellow corn to Asian nations including Malaysia, South Korea and the Philippines. A USDA official on Thursday estimated recent Chinese corn sales to be at least 300,000 tonnes.
Some exporters were not overly concerned about China's reentry into the corn export business.
"Everybody has been expecting China to get back into the market," said one U.S. corn exporter. "Really, it's nothing much for the market."
